971.event_title: Emil Zatopek wins the 5,000 metres, 10,000 metres and marathon at one Olympics
971.event: Emil Zatopek, a Czechoslovak runner who had taken up the sport while working in a shoe factory and was nicknamed the Human Locomotive for his relentless training, built his success on a punishing interval-training method that others at first scoffed at. At the 1952 Olympic Games in Helsinki he won the 10,000 metres and then the 5,000 metres, both in Olympic record times, and then entered the marathon, a race he had never run before, and won it by more than two and a half minutes. No athlete before or since has won all three long-distance events at the same Games.
971.explanation: Zatopek's triple victory is remembered as one of the greatest feats in athletics, and it grew from his drive to train harder than anyone thought sensible.
971.tie_back: The kural says a person's true glory is an abundance of inner drive and his disgrace is the thought of getting through life without it, and Zatopek's achievement came from exactly that inner zeal.
971._accuracy_note: A vivid case of greatness springing from inner drive; the kural's contrasting disgrace of the slack is not shown.

972.event_title: Zhu Yuanzhang, an orphaned peasant and beggar monk, founds the Ming dynasty
972.event: Zhu Yuanzhang was born in 1328 into a poor farming family in Haozhou, and when he was a teenager his parents and brothers died, leaving him to enter a Buddhist monastery to avoid starvation and then to wander as a begging monk when the temple could no longer feed him. He joined a rebel army against the Mongol Yuan dynasty at about twenty-four, rose to command, educated himself with the help of scholars, and defeated rival leaders. In 1368 he proclaimed himself emperor at Nanjing, taking the reign title Hongwu, and founded the Ming dynasty, which ruled China for 276 years.
972.explanation: A boy with no family, land or schooling rose by his own deeds to found one of China's great dynasties, though his later rule became harsh and despotic.
972.tie_back: The kural says all are equal by birth and that distinction differs only by the deeds people do, and Zhu's humble birth did not prevent his deeds from making him emperor.
972._accuracy_note: A classic illustration that distinction comes from deeds rather than birth; his despotic later reign means his deeds were not all admirable.

973.event_title: The former slave Epictetus becomes the most admired Stoic teacher of his age
973.date: c. 55 to c. 135 CE (school at Nicopolis from about 90 CE)
973.place: Rome, Italy, and Nicopolis, Epirus, Greece
973.event: Epictetus was born around 55 CE in Hierapolis in Phrygia and as a boy was brought to Rome as a slave of Epaphroditus, a rich freedman who had served the emperor Nero; while still enslaved he attended the lectures of the Stoic Musonius Rufus. After he was freed, he was expelled from Rome around 89-90 CE when the emperor Domitian banished the philosophers, and he opened a school at Nicopolis in Greece that attracted upper-class Roman students, including Arrian, who wrote down his teachings as the Discourses and the Handbook. Later writers report that he was more popular in his own day than Plato. The tutor of the future emperor Marcus Aurelius, Herodes Atticus, is reported to have called him the greatest of the Stoics.
973.explanation: Born into the lowest rank of Roman society and lame for much of his life, Epictetus became one of the most influential moral teachers of the ancient world, while the emperor who banished him is remembered as a tyrant.
973.tie_back: The kural says that those who are not base are not low even when placed low, and Epictetus, a slave by station, stood morally far above many who sat on high seats.
973._accuracy_note: Fits the kural's second half almost exactly; the first half, about the unworthy on high seats, is illustrated only by the passing contrast with Domitian.

974.event_title: Lou Gehrig plays 2,130 consecutive games and then takes himself out of the lineup
974.event: From 1 June 1925 the New York Yankees first baseman Lou Gehrig played in every one of his team's games for almost fourteen years, a record of 2,130 consecutive games that stood until 1995. A quiet and modest man often overshadowed by his flamboyant teammate Babe Ruth, he was remembered by a teammate as someone who simply did his job every day. When his play declined badly at the start of the 1939 season because of the illness later diagnosed as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Gehrig himself took his name out of the lineup on 2 May 1939, ending the streak, and he never played again.
974.explanation: Gehrig's greatness rested on steady self-discipline sustained over years, and he guarded his own standards even to the point of ending his record himself.
974.tie_back: The kural says that greatness, like a woman's single-hearted faithfulness, belongs only to one who guards himself, and Gehrig's record was the fruit of a self-discipline no one else imposed on him.
974._accuracy_note: Illustrates self-kept discipline as the source of greatness, but the kural's comparison is to chastity and moral self-guarding, which a sporting record only approximates.

975.event_title: Galileo, under house arrest and going blind, completes Two New Sciences
975.place: Siena and Arcetri, near Florence, Italy, and Leiden, Netherlands
975.event: After his condemnation by the Inquisition in 1633, Galileo began assembling his Discourses on Two New Sciences while confined in Siena, and continued it under house arrest at his villa in Arcetri, where in 1634 he also lost his beloved daughter Maria Celeste. Because publishing in Italy was closed to him, the Dutch printer Louis Elzevir visited him in 1636 and agreed to print the book in Leiden; by January 1638 Galileo had lost his sight entirely. The book came off the press in July 1638, founding the science of the strength of materials and setting out his laws of motion, the pendulum and the parabolic path of projectiles.
975.explanation: Stripped of freedom, family and finally sight, the old Galileo still produced the work often regarded as the foundation of modern physics.
975.tie_back: The kural says that the great accomplish, in the proper way, deeds that are hard for others, and Galileo completed his hardest scientific work when his circumstances were at their worst.
975._accuracy_note: A strong match, especially with the traditional reading that the great achieve hard things even when reduced in circumstances.

976.event_title: James Boswell seeks out Samuel Johnson and becomes his biographer
976.place: Thomas Davies's bookshop, Russell Street, Covent Garden, London, England
976.event: The young Scottish lawyer James Boswell, who had admired Samuel Johnson's writings for years, spent months in London trying to meet him and finally did so on 16 May 1763 in the back parlour of the bookseller Thomas Davies, where Johnson's sharp replies left him embarrassed. Undeterred, Boswell called on Johnson at his lodgings a week later and cultivated the friendship for twenty-one years, recording Johnson's conversation in remarkable detail in his journals. His Life of Samuel Johnson, published in 1791, is regarded as one of the greatest biographies in English.
976.explanation: Boswell's determination to learn from a great man and preserve his words gave the world its fullest portrait of Johnson.
976.tie_back: The kural says that the resolve to cherish the great and make their way one's own never arises in small minds, and Boswell's persistent pursuit of Johnson is the very resolve the kural says the small lack.
976._accuracy_note: Illustrates the kural from the positive side, showing the aspiration the small-minded lack, rather than showing small minds failing to aspire.

977.event_title: Mobutu Sese Seko builds his palace city at Gbadolite
977.place: Gbadolite, Zaire (now Democratic Republic of the Congo)
977.event: Mobutu Sese Seko seized power in Zaire in 1965 and, while corruption and mismanagement led the country into decline, amassed one of the largest personal fortunes in the world. In his home region of Gbadolite he built three palaces lined with Italian marble, guest houses for the world's rich and famous, Chinese pagodas, a private hydroelectric plant and an airstrip for the Concorde airliner he frequently used, a complex nicknamed the Versailles of the Jungle. After he was overthrown in 1997 the palaces were looted and now stand in ruins in one of the poorest countries on earth.
977.explanation: The highest office in a vast nation became, in Mobutu's hands, a means to lavish excess while its people grew poorer.
977.tie_back: The kural says that distinction falling to the unworthy turns into deeds that overstep every limit, and supreme office in Mobutu's hands produced the boundless extravagance of Gbadolite.
977._accuracy_note: A strong modern example of power in unworthy hands running to excess; the precise construction dates of the palaces are not given in the sources consulted.

978.event_title: Hokusai, at seventy-five, declares that nothing he drew before seventy was worth noticing
978.event: By 1834 Katsushika Hokusai was already famous for his print series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, including the Great Wave, yet in a postscript to the first volume of his illustrated book One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji, written at the age of seventy-five, he declared that nothing he had drawn before seventy was worthy of notice. He wrote that only at seventy-three had he begun to grasp the structure of plants, birds, animals, insects and fish, and that he hoped to keep improving through eighty, ninety and a hundred until, at a hundred and ten, every dot and stroke would be alive. He signed himself the Old Man Mad About Painting, and on his deathbed in 1849 he still wished for a few more years in which to become a true artist.
978.explanation: Japan's most celebrated artist, at the height of his fame, judged his own work with humility and saw himself as still a learner.
978.tie_back: The kural says that greatness always bows in humility while littleness decks itself out in self-admiration, and the great Hokusai dismissed his own famous work as only a beginning.
978._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of greatness bowing in humility; the contrasting self-admiring littleness is not shown.

979.event_title: Pierre and Marie Curie decline the Legion of Honour
979.event: Pierre and Marie Curie, who shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics for their work on radioactivity, made it a rule to refuse state decorations, while gladly accepting scientific prizes and memberships for their work. Pierre Curie declined France's Legion of Honour in the years before his death in 1906. In 1910, when the minister of education proposed that Marie Curie receive it, she politely declined as well, keeping to the rule she had adopted with her husband.
979.explanation: Two of the most celebrated scientists in the world saw no need for ornaments of rank, valuing only the recognition of their work itself.
979.tie_back: The kural says greatness is the absence of arrogance while littleness rides on pride, and the Curies, with every reason for pride, refused the decorations that others coveted.
979._accuracy_note: A good example of eminence without self-display; the exact year of Pierre's refusal is not stated in the sources consulted.

980.event_title: Eisenhower writes a note taking all the blame if D-Day fails
980.place: England, United Kingdom (Allied command for the Normandy invasion)
980.event: On 5 June 1944, after giving the final order for the Allied invasion of Normandy, General Dwight D. Eisenhower wrote a short statement to be issued if the landings failed, saying that the troops had been withdrawn and that his decision had been based on the best information available. He praised the soldiers, airmen and sailors for their bravery and devotion to duty and ended with the words, "If any blame or fault attaches to the attempt it is mine alone." The invasion succeeded, the note was never issued, and an aide retrieved it after Eisenhower discarded it; in his haste Eisenhower had misdated it July 5.
980.explanation: The Supreme Allied Commander prepared, in advance, to shield everyone under him and to carry any failure himself.
980.tie_back: The kural says greatness covers up the weaknesses of others while littleness speaks only of their faults, and Eisenhower was ready to hide any failings of his forces behind his own acceptance of the blame.
980._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of shielding others' failings; since the invasion succeeded, the cover he offered was never actually needed.
